16. The High Court did acknowledge the Employer's inability to justify these abrupt terminations. 
Consequently, it ordered re-engagement on daily wages with some measure of parity in minimum pay. 
Regrettably, this only perpetuated precariousness: the Appellant Workmen were left in a marginally 
improved yet still uncertain status. While the High Court recognized the importance of their work and hinted 
at eventual regularization, it failed to afford them continuity of service or meaningful back wages 
commensurate with the degree of statutory violation evident on record. 


17. In light of these considerations, the Employer's discontinuation of the Appellant Workmen stands in 
violation of the most basic labour law principles. Once it is established that their services were terminated 
without adhering to Sections 6E and 6N of the U.P. Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and that they were 
engaged in essential, perennial duties, these workers cannot be relegated to perpetual uncertainty. While 
concerns of municipal budget and compliance with recruitment rules merit consideration, such concerns do 
not absolve the Employer of statutory obligations or negate equitable entitlements. Indeed, bureaucratic 
limitations cannot trump the legitimate rights of workmen who have served continuously in de facto regular 
roles for an extended period. 


18. The impugned order of the High Court, to the extent they confine the Appellant Workmen to future daily- 
wage engagement without continuity or meaningful back wages, is hereby set aside with the following 
directions: 


I. The discontinuation of the Appellant Workmen's services, effected without compliance with Section 6E and 
Section 60 of the U.P. Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, is declared illegal. All orders o2 communications 
terminating their services are quashed. In consequence, the Appellant Workmen shall be treated as 
continuing in service from the date of their termination, for all purposes, including seniority and continuity 
in service. 


II. The Respondent Employer shall reinstate the Appellant Workmen in their respective posts (or posts akin 
to the duties they previously performed) within four weeks from the date of this judgment. Their entire period 
of absence (from the date of termination until actual reinstatement) shall be counted for continuity of service 
and all consequential benefits, such as seniority and eligibility for promotions, if any. 


III. Considering the length of service, the Appellant Workmen shall be entitled to 50% of the back wages 
from the date of their discontinuation until their actual reinstatement. The Respondent Employer shall clear 
the aforesaid dues within three months from the date of their reinstatement. 


IV. The Respondent Employer is directed to initiate a fair and transparent process for regularizing the 
Appellant Workmen within six months from the date of reinstatement, duly considering the fact that they have 
performed perennial municipal duties akin to permanent posts. In assessing regularization, the Employer 
shall not impose educational or procedural criteria retroactively if such requirements were never applied to 
the Appellant Workmen or to similarly situated regular employees in the past. To the extent that sanctioned 
vacancies for such duties exist or are required, the Respondent Employer shall expedite all necessary 
administrative processes to ensure these longtime employees are not indefinitely retained on daily wages 
contrary to statutory and equitable norms. 


It is relevant to mention herein while passing the said judgment by the Hon’ble Division Bench of the Supreme Court 
it was not brought to the notice that earlier on the point in issue Hon’ble three judges bench in the case of Madhyamik 
Siksha Parishad, UP. Vs. Anil Kumar Mishra & Others Etc, reported in AIRI994SC1638, held as under:- 


4. We are unable to uphold the order of the High Court. There were no sanctioned posts in existence to 
which they could be said to have been appointed. The assignment was an ad hoc one which anticipated spent 
itself out. It is difficult to envisage for them, the status of workmen on the analogy of the provisions of 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, importing the incidents of completion of 240 days' work. The legal 
consequences that flow from work for that duration under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 are entirely 
different from what, by way of implication, is attributed to the present situation by way of analogy. The 
completion of 240 days' work does not, under that law import the right to regularisation. It merely imposes 
certain obligations on the employer at the time of termination of the service. It is not appropriate to import 
and apply that analogy, in an extended or enlarged form here. 


The Hon’ble three Judges Bench in the case of Manager, RBI, Bangalore vs. S. Mani & Ors reported in 2005 (SC) 
100, held as under relevant portion quoted herein below:- 


In law, 240 days of continuous service by itself does not give rise to claim of permanence. Section 25F 
provides for grant of compensation if a workman is sought to be retrenched in violation of the conditions 
referred to therein. [See Maharashtra State Cooperative Cotton Growers' Marketing Federation Ltd.(supra). 
See also Madhyamik Siksha Parishad, U.P. Vs. Anil Kumar Mishra and others, etc., AIR 1994 SC 1638] In 
A. Umarani (supra), this Court held: 


794 


THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : FEBRUARY 14, 2026/MAGHA 25, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


"Regularisation, in our considered opinion, is not and cannot be the mode of recruitment by any 
"State" within the meaning of Article 12 of the Constitution of India or any body or authority 
governed by a Statutory Act or the Rules framed thereunder. It is also now well- settled that an 
appointment made in violation of the mandatory provisions of the Statute and in particular ignoring 
the minimum educational qualification and other essential qualification would be wholly illegal. 
Such illegality cannot be cured by taking recourse to regularisation. (See State of H.P. Vs. Suresh 
Kumar Verma and Another, (1996) 7 SCC 562)." 


Yet again, in Executive Engineer, ZP Engg. Divn. And Another Vs. Digambara Rao and Others [(2004) 8 
SCC 262] this Court held: 


"It may not be out of place to mention that completion of 240 days of continuous service in a year 
may not by itself be a ground for directing an order of regularization. It is also not the case of the 
Respondents that they were appointed in accordance with the extant rules. No direction for 
regularization of their services was, therefore, could be issued." 


Furthermore, a direction for reinstatement for non- compliance of the provisions of Section 25F of the 
Industrial Disputes Act would restore to the workmen the same status which he held when terminated. The 
Respondents would, thus, continue to be Ticca Mazdoors, meaning thereby their names would continue in 
the second list. They had worked only from April, 1980 to December, 1982. They did not have any right to 
get work. The direction of continuity of service per se would not bring them within the purview of terms of 
settlement. Even in the case of a statutory corporation in S.G. Kotturappa (supra), this Court observed: 


"It is not a case where the Respondent has completed 240 days of service during the period of 12 
months preceding such termination as contemplated under Section 25- F read with Section 25-B of 
the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The Badli workers, thus, did not acquire any legal right to 
continue in service. They were not even entitled to the protection under the Industrial Disputes Act 
nor the mandatory requirements of Section 25-F of the Industrial Disputes were required to be 
complied with before terminating his services, unless they complete 240 days service within a 
period of twelve months preceding the date of termination." 


It was further held: 


"The terms and conditions of employment of a Badli worker may have a statutory flavour but the 
same would not mean that it is not otherwise contractual. So long as a worker remains a Badli 
worker, he does not enjoy a status. His services are not protected by reason of any provisions of the 
statute. He does not hold a civil post. A dispute as regard purported wrongful termination of 
services can be raised only if such termination takes place in violation of the mandatory provisions 
of the statute governing the services. Services of a temporary employee or a badli worker can be 
terminated upon compliance of the contractual or statutory requirements." 


Mr. Phadke, as noticed hereinbefore, has referred to a large number of decisions for demonstrating that this 
Court had directed reinstatement even if the workmen concerned were daily wagers or were employed 
intermittently. No proposition of law was laid down in the aforementioned judgments. The said judgments of 
this Court, moreover, do not lay down any principle having universal application so that the Tribunals, or 
for that matter the High Court, or this Court, may feel compelled to direct reinstatement with continuity of 
service and backwages. The Tribunal has some discretion in this matter. Grant of relief must depend on the 
fact situation obtaining in a particular case. The industrial adjudicator cannot be held to be bound to grant 
some relief only because it will be lawful to do so. 


In Haryana State Coop. Land Dev. Bank Vs. Neelam [JT 2005 (2) SC 600], this Court observed: 


"It is trite that the courts and tribunals having plenary jurisdiction have discretionary power to 
grant an appropriate relief to the parties. The aim and object of the Industrial Disputes Act may be 
to impart social justice to the workman but the same by itself would not mean that irrespective of 
his conduct a workman would automatically be entitled to relief. The procedural laws like estoppel, 
waiver and acquiescence are equally applicable to the industrial proceedings. A person in certain 
situation may even be held to be bound by the doctrine of Acceptance Sub silentio." 


OTHER CONTENTIONS: 
We have noticed hereinbefore that the Appellant herein raised a specific plea denying or disputing the claim 
of the Respondents that they had completed 240 days of work. Such a ales havina haen mised hath before the 


Industrial Tribunal as also before the High Court, we cannot accept that the Appellant had abandoned such 
a plea. Even in this Special Leave Petition, it is contended: 


"(3)For that the High Court ought to have held that the disengagement of the Ticca Mazdoors 
(Respondents), who were daily wage casual workers, did not involve any retrenchment and as such 
there was no question of reinstatement of Respondents will full backwages from 23.7.1993." 


[भाग त---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : फरवरी 14, 2026/ माघ 25, 1947 795 


Further the Hon’ble Two Judges Bench of Apex Court in the case of Ghaziabad Development Authority & Anr ys. 
Ashok Kumar & Anr reported in 2008 (4) SCC 261, held that in a subsequent case of retrenchment without 
complying with statutory requirement, the Labour Court directed reinstatement with full wages. On appeal, the 
Supreme Court held that Labour Court did not notice that they could not be reinstated despite the fact that they were 
working continuously for more than 240 days in a year as further sanction from the State Government was wanting. 
The Court therefore directed to pay compensation of 50,000. 


And the Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Vibhuti Shankar Pandey vs. The State of mandhya Pradesh & Ors, 
(Arising Out of SLP (C) No.10519 of 2020, vide judgment dated 08.02.2023, relevant paragraph quoted herein 
below:- 


3. The case of the appellant is that he was engaged in Digitally signed by NIRMALA NEGI 1980 as a 
Supervisor, on daily rated basis, under a project Date: 2023.02.08 16:38:38 IST Reason: of the State Water 
Resources Department of Madhya Pradesh. The appellant sought regularization on the post of 
Supervisor/Time Keeper. Admittedly, the minimum qualification for the said post was matriculation with 
mathematics; a qualification which the appellant did not possess. These qualifications were relaxed by a 
Government Circular dated 31.12.2010 and the appellant sought his regularization on the post of 
Supervisor/Time Keeper, as he was qualified for the post and had been working on daily wage basis for a 
long period of time. In fact, in another writ petition (W.P. 13997/2010) filed by the appellant earlier, the 
High Court of Madhya Pradesh vide order dated 02.11.2017, had given directions to the State Government 
to decide the claim of the writ petitioner in accordance with law. Vide order dated 18.06.2018 issued by the 
Office of Chief Engineer, Rani Avanti Bai Lodhi Sagar Project, the claim of the appellant for regularization 
was rejected for the reasons that though the minimum qualifications of matriculation with mathematics will 
not come in the way for his regularization, but the fact remains that the appellant was never appointed 
against any post. Moreover, his appointment was never made by the competent authority and there were no 
posts available at the time for regularization. The appellant on the other hand, had set his claim for 
regularization as persons who were junior to him as daily wagers were regularized in the year 1990 or even 
before. The learned Single Judge while allowing the writ petition gave directions for regularization of the 
appellant from the date on which his juniors were regularized. This order was challenged by the State 
Government before a Division Bench which allowed the appeal of the State Government. The Division Bench 
rightly held that the learned Single Judge has not followed the principle of law as given by this Court in 
Secretary, State of Karnataka and Ors. v. Umadevi and Ors. 1 (2006) 4 SCC 1, as initial appointment must 
be done by the competent authority and there must be a sanctioned post on which the daily rated employee 
must be working. These two conditions were clearly missing in the case of the present appellant. The 
Division Bench of the High Court therefore has to our mind rightly allowed the appeal and set aside the 
order dated 27.06.2019. 


Taking into consideration the above said facts/position of law and the Latin expression “Per Incuriam” means 
through inadvertence. A decision can be said generally to be given “Per Incuriam” when the Supreme Court has 
acted in ignorance of a previous decision of its own or when a High Court has acted in ignorance of a decision of the 
Supreme Court. As regards the judgments of the Supreme Court allegedly rendered in ignorance of a relevant 
constitutional provision or other statutory provisions on the subjects covered by them, the Supreme Court may not be 
said to "declare the law" on those subjects if the relevant provisions were not really present to its mind. The problem 
of judgment per incuriam when actually arises, should present no difficulty as the Supreme Court can lay down the 
law afresh, if two or more of its earlier judgments cannot stand together. Article 141, which embodies, as a rule of 
law, the doc- trine of precedents, was enacted to make the law declared by the Supreme Court binding on all courts in 
the country excluding, as is now being interpreted, the Supreme Court itself, in the case of Punjab Land 
Development and Recalmation Corp.Ltd vs. Presiding Officer, (1990) 3 SCC 682, (see also in State of UP ys. 
Synthetics and Chemicals Ltd, (1991) 4 SCC 139, and in Siddharam Satlingappa Mhetre vs. State of Maharashtra, 
(2011) I SCC 694). 


Further Hon’ble Andhra Pradesh High Court in the case of The Depot Manager, APSRTC vs. Ponnapati Venkata 
Ramana & Others, 2024 LLR 497, held as under relevant portion quoted herein below:- 


12. The learned counsel for corporation placed reliance on Managing Director Ajmer Vidhyut Vitran Nigam 
Ltd Ajmer & Anr v. Chiggan Lal and Ors., 2022 LawSuit (SC) 337, the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India held 
that the date from which regularization is to be granted is the matter to be decided by the employer keeping 
in view a number of factors like nature of the work, numbers posts vacant, the financial condition of the 
employer, the additional financial burden caused, the suitability of the work- men for job, the manner in 
which the initial appoint was made etc, the said decision will also depend on facts of each year and no parity 
can be claimed based on regularization made in respect of the earlier years and also relied on Union Bank 
of India v. Ilmo Devi & Anr., 2021 Law Suit (SC) 614, the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India held that 
regularization policy to regularize the services of employees working on temporary status and/or casual 
laborers is the policy decision and in judicial review the Courts cannot issue mandamus directions when 
there is no post. Mere continuation of service by a temporary or ad hoc or daily wage employee, under cover 


796 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : FEBRUARY 14, 2026/MAGHA 25, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


of interim orders of the Court would not confer upon him any right to be absorb into service as such service 
would be litigious employment. Even temporary, ad hoc or daily wage service for a long number of years let 
alone service for one or two years, will not entitle such employee to claim regularization, if he is not working 
against a sanctioned post. Sympathy and sentiment cannot be the basis for passing any order in absence of 
any legal right. 


Recently Hon’ble Punjab & Haryana High Court in the case of Mandip Singh @Mandeep Singh vs. D.B 
Corporation. Pvt. Ltd & Another, 2025 (187) FLR 888, on the point in issue has held as under, relevant portion 
quoted herein below:- 


34. The reasons for denying the relief of reinstatement in such cases are obvious. It is trite law that when the 
termination is found to be illegal because of non-payment of retrenchment compensation and notice pay as 
mandatorily required under Section 25-F of the Industrial Disputes Act, even after reinstatement, it is always 
open to the management to terminate the services of that employee by paying him the retrenchment 
compensation. Since such a workman was working on daily-wage basis and even after he is reinstated, he 
has no right to seek regularisation [see State of Karnataka v. Umadevi (3)], Thus when he cannot claim 
regularisation and he has no right to continue even as a daily-wage worker, no useful purpose is going to be 
served in reinstating such a workman and he can be given monetary compensation by the Court itself 
inasmuch as if he is terminated again after reinstatement, he would receive monetary compensation only in 
the form of retrenchment. compensation and notice pay." 


This principle has been reiterated by the Supreme Court in its judgment in the case of State of Uttarakhand 
v. Raj Kumar, 2019 (160) FLR 791 (SC). 


6. It is, thus, manifest that the Court can mould the relief and direct payment of compensation commensurate 
with the number of years put in service by the workman. Reliance can be placed on the judgment of this 
Court in the case of Sukhbir Singh v. State of Haryana and others, LPA No. 1203 of 2021 decided on 
01.03.2023, whereafter after relying upon the law laid down by the Supreme Court in several cases, the 
Court had arrived at the conclusion that the compensation of ¢50,000/- for every year of service rendered by 
the workman, would meet the ends of justice. The relevant extract of the judgment is reproduced hereunder: 


"5. It is to be noticed that as per the demand notice itself the claim that he had been appointed in 
the said post in a different district at Gurugram from 01.02.1993 to 31.12.1993 and thereafter, 
accommodated at Rohtak and had continued till 21.09.1994 and was adjusted at District Jhajjar 
apparently on the creation of the same from 31.09.1996 and resultantly, retrenched on 19.11.1998 
and therefore, had completed 240 days of service. Similar was the claim statement made and in the 
written statement it was admitted that he had worked from 01.03.1993 and continued as claimed 
and had been transferred to Jhajjar on 19.12.1997 for the period from to 27.02.1998 and from 
16.06.1998 to 12.09.1998 and from to 19.11.1998. The finding recorded by the Labour Court while 
placing reliance upon Ext.M-3 the detail of the working days prepared was that he had worked from 
01.12.1997 upto 19.11.1998 for a period of 245 days. There was neither any such defence by the 
State also that it was a case under Section 2(00)(bb) of the Act and this aspect also missed the 
attention of the learned Single Judge. It has been time and again held that until there is a perversity 
in the award the Writ Court is not to sit as a Court of appeal and interfere in the orders under 
Article 226/227 of the Constitution of India. Reliance can be placed upon the judgment of Apex 
Court passed in K.V.S. Ram ७9. Bangalore Metropolitan Transport Corporation, 2015 (144) FLR 
994 (SC). 


6. Resultantly, once the workman had completed 240 days and apparently had worked for a period 
spanning more than 3-14 years, we are of the considered opinion that dispensing of his service 
before his contractual period came to an end would entitle him for the statutory protection which 
would be evident from the award of the Labour Court. However, keeping in view the fact that at this 
point of time, it would not be justified to put him back in service since a period of almost 25 years 
has gone by and therefore, it would be just and appropriate to award compensation to the tune of 
2,50,000/- on an average of 50,000/- per year, keeping in view the fact that the State had taken his 
service for more than 5 years with the same office in different districts." 


7. In the afore-noted facts and circumstances, when the appellant had worked for about three years, the 
compensation of 2 Lakhs appears to be justified. Consequently, we do not find any merit in this Letters 
Patent Appeal which stands dismissed. 


And The Hon’ble Madhya Pradesh High Court, Gwalior Bench in the case of Mahesh Singh Bhadoria vs. Muncipal 
Council, Akoda, 2025 (187) FLR 873, held that relevant paragraphs quoted herein below:- 


13. After hearing learned counsel for the parties and going through the records. Law in regard to 
reinstatement and compensation in lieu of reinstatement has been settled by the Supreme Court to a great 
extent. The labour Court has admitted a fact that retrenchment of the petitioner/workman was illegal. There 
is no appeal to challenge this finding of the Labour Court. 


[भाग [avs 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : फरवरी 14, 2026/ माघ 25, 1947 797 


14, M.P. High Court in the case of Rupendra Joshi v. Municipal Rupendra Joshi, has discussed this aspect 
and has upheld the compensation in lieu of reinstatement based on illegal termination and lack of 
entitlement for regularization. 


15. Law in regard to the aforesaid subject is crystal clear as laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of 
Harinandan Prasad v. Employer I/R To Management of FCI, wherein the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held 
that when the termination is set-aside because of violation of Section 25-F of the Industrial Disputes Act, it is 
not necessary that relief of reinstatement be also given as a matter of right. Same is the ratio of law in the 
case of Jayant Vasant Rao Hiwarkar v. Anoop Ganpat Rao Bobade, and Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited v. 
Bhurumal. 


16. However, looking to the fact that workman had worked for a long duration, this Court is of the opinion 
that grant of compensation of 1,50,000/-is not sufficient. 


17. In fact, in case of Ramesh Chand v. Management of Delhi Transport Corporation (Civil Appeal No. 4208 
of 2023) Arising out of SLP (Civil) No. 7137 of 2016 Hon'ble Supreme Court vide its decision dated 
05.07.2023 awarded a sum of 3,00,000/- to the appellant therein in lieu of back- wages. In that case, 
however, order of reinstatement was passed. 


18. But in the present case, looking to the timeline of about more than nine years, when retrenchment took 
place till the date and time period which has lapsed till now, it will be appropriate to direct that respondent- 
authority shall pay a sum of 2,50,000/- (Rupees Two Lacs Fifty Thousand only) to the workman- petitioner in 
lieu of reinstatement, in place of 1,50,000/- as has been awarded by the learned Labour Court. After 
adjusting the amounts, if any, already paid, remaining amount of compensation be paid to the petitioner/ 
workman within a period of 45 days from the date of receipt of certified copy of this order. 


Thus in so far as the claim of the employee for regularization of his services is concerned as held by the Hon'ble 
Supreme Court, the employee has to establish that he was working in any sanctioned post or against the vacancy. It is 
also not the case of the employee that her appointment is in pursuance of a regular recruitment in accordance with 
relevant rules. 


Further it is well settled proposition that an employee who has been appointed through back door methods or 
appointed contrary to the constitutional scheme cannot be regularized. It is also settled law that mere continuation of 
service by temporary employee under cover of an order of the Court would not automatically entitled the employee to 
be absorbed into service. 


Taking to consideration the position of law on point in issue as well as the fact that the workman has established that 
he worked more than 240 days in 12 months in preceding on calendar year prior to date of his 
retrenchment/termination on 26.02.2005. 


Accordingly, workman/Shri Ramendra Kumar alias chotu, is entitled for retrenchment compensation but not for 
reinstatement in service. 


AWARD 


For the forgoing reasons I.D case filed by workman/Shri Ramendra Kumar alias chotu, u/s 2A of the Industrial 
Disputed Act 1947, is partly allowed and workman is entitled for retrenchment compensation as his service was 
retrenched on 26.02.2005, with complying the provision of Section 25F of the Act amounting to Rs.3,00,000/-(Three 
Lakhs only). 


However, he is not entitled of reinstatement in service.

“Whether the action of M/s. Master Marine Services Pvt. Ltd., in transferring Shri Manoj Upadhyay, Sr.

AWARD 
(Delivered on 18-12-2025) 


1. This Reference has been made by the Central Government in exercise of powers under clause (9) of 
sub-section (1) and sub-section (2A) of Section 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, vide Government of India, 
Ministry of Labour & Employment, New Delhi, order No. L-12025/04/2016 (IR(B-II) dated 05.09.2016. The terms of 
reference given in the schedule are as follows: 


“Whether the action of the management of Central Bank of India, Central Office, Mumbai (i) in 
withdrawing the special leave facility for attending executive committee meetings and trinial conference, 
(ii) in withdrawing the joint discussion facility, (iii) in withdrawing the nomination of the union in the Staff 
Welfare Committee, and (iv) in withdrawing the mercy appeal facility to the delinquent employees 
aggrieved by the decisions of departmental enquiry etc, by revising the existing norms and introduction of 
new rules of discipline, are amounting to violation of Section 9 A of the ILD. Act, 1947 read with Item No. 6 
and 9 of 4" Schedule of the said Act? If so, what relief the All India Central Bank Employees’ Congress 
and their member workmen concerned are entitled to?” 


2. The case is called out today. The Learned Counsel for the respondent Ms. Deepika Agrawal is present before 
the Court, but no one is present on behalf of the petitioner. From perusal of record, it is apparent that, the petitioner is 
not responding and attending the Court since 05.05.2021 long back. Although, Statement of Claim has been filed by 
the petitioner, but no Written Statement has been filed by the respondent till today. No other evidence has been filed 
by the petitioner to prove his case. The petitioner is not coming to the Court since long back. It appears that, the 
petitioner is not interested to contest the case furthermore. The claim of the petitioner is not proved. So, the case is 
closed. 


Hence, it is ordered. 
ORDER 


The action of the management of Central Bank of India, Central Office, Mumbai (i) in withdrawing 
the special leave facility for attending executive committee meetings and trinial conference, (ii) in 
withdrawing the joint discussion facility, (iii) in withdrawing the nomination of the union in the Staff 
Welfare Committee, and (iv) in withdrawing the mercy appeal facility to the delinquent employees 
aggrieved by the decisions of departmental enquiry etc, by revising the existing norms and 
introduction of new rules of discipline, are not amounting to violation of Section 9 A of the I.D. Act, 
1947 read with Item No. 8 and 9 of 47 Schedule of the said Act. The All India Central Bank 
Employees’ Congress and their concerned member workmen are not entitled to any relief.

सं. 1 प्रेस/2026--राष्ट्रपति, स्वतंत्रता दिवस, 2025 के अवसर पर, 0629-डी, समादेशक श्रीनिवास गदम को वीरता के लिए तटरक्षक 
पदक सहर्ष प्रदान करते हैं। 


प्रशस्ति उल्लेख 


1. 0629-डी, समादेशक श्रीनिवास गदम भारतीय तटरक्षक के एक अनुभवी अधिकारी हैं। वे 29 जनवरी 2002 को सेवा में शामिल 
हुए और वर्तमान में 840 स्क्वाड्रन (तटरक्षक) के कमान अधिकारी के रुप में कार्यरत हैं। 16 वर्षों से अधिक के उड़ान अनुभव और 2000 घंटे से 
अधिक दुर्घटना-मुकत्त उड़ान तथा इंस्ट्रूमेंट रेटिंग/कैट मास्टर ग्रीन AY के साथ, उक्त अधिकारी ने लगातार असाधारण पेशेवर और परिचालन 
कौशल का प्रदर्शन किया है। 


2. दिनांक 28 नवंबर 2024 को, जब विनाशकारी चक्रवात फेंगल तमिलनाडु तट की तरफ बढ़ रहा था, तब मुख्यालय तटरक्षक क्षेत्र 
पूर्व को तमिलनाडु राज्य के अधिकारियों से दोपहर 1410 बजे एक संकटकालीन कॉल प्राप्त हुई, जिसमें बताया गया कि कुट्टालोर के पास 10 
मछुआरे अपनी नावों के नष्ट हो जाने के बाद समुद्र में फँस गए हैं। प्रतिकूल मौसम, अत्यंत खराब दृश्यता और परिचालन सीमाओं के बावजूद, 
अधिकारी ने निस्वार्थ साहस और दृढ़ नेतृत्व का उदाहरण प्रस्तुत करते हुए, प्रथम-प्रतिक्रिया हवाई बचाव अभियान का नेतृत्व करने के लिए 
स्वेच्छा से आगे आए। 

3. असाधारण परिचालन योजना का प्रदर्शन करते हुए, अधिकारी ने ईंधन आवश्यकताओं और मिशन मापदंडो का सावधानीपूर्वक 
आकलन किया और बचाव स्थल पर अधिकतम स्थिरता सुनिश्चित की। 1515 बजे, ए एल एच एम के-॥॥ हेलीकॉप्टर ने चेन्नई अंतराष्ट्रीय हवाई 
अड्डे से उड़ान भरी। लगातार मौसम व्यवधानों, भारी बारिश और तेज़ हवाओं के बीच, अधिकारी ने त्रुटिहीन चालक दल संसाधन प्रबंधन (सी 
आर एम) और निर्बाध चालक दल समन्वय का प्रदर्शन किया। 

4. बचाव स्थल पर पहुँचने पर, टीम को 50 समुद्री मील से अधिक तूफानी हवाओं, शक्ति प्रयोग के कम दायरे और खतरनाक रुप से 
ऊंची समुद्री लहरों का सामना करना पड़ा। निडर होकर, अधिकारी ने प्रचंड सटीक होवर और कई विंचिंग ऑपरेशन किए। उनकी दृढ़ता और 
उड़ान कौशल के परिणामस्वरुप सभी 10 जीवित बचे लोगों को समुद्र में होने वाली मृत्यु से सफलतापूर्वक बचाया गया। 

5. इस अधिकारी के असाधारण साहस, उत्कृष्ट वायु कौशल और जीवन के लिए खतरनाक परिस्थितियों में भी कर्तव्य के प्रति अटूट 
प्रतिबद्धता ने भारतीय तटरक्षक को अपार सम्मान दिलाया। 

6. उनकी असाधारण वीरता, अटूट संकल्प और उत्कृष्ट नेतृत्व के लिए, 0629-डी, समादेशक श्रीनिवास गदम ने स्वयं को बखूबी सिद्ध

PRESIDENT’S SECRETARIAT 
New Delhi, the 15th August 2025 


No. 1-Pres/2026—The President is pleased to award the Tatrakshak Medal for Gallantry to 0629-D, Commandant 
Srinivas Gadam on the occasion of the Independence Day, 2025. 


CITATION 
1. 0629-D, Commandant Srinivas Gadam is an experienced officer of Indian Coast Guard, joined the service on 29 
January 2002 and is presently serving as the Commanding Officer of 840 Squadron (Coast Guard). With over 16 years of flying 


experience and more than 2000 hours of accident-free flying, coupled with Instrument Rating/CAT Master Green ‘B’, the 
officer has consistently demonstrated exceptional professionalism and operational acumen. 


2. On 28 November 2024, as the devastating Cyclone Fengal battered the Tamil Nadu coast, Headquarters Coast 
Guard Region East received a distress call at 1410 hours from Tamil Nadu State authorities reporting 10 fishermen stranded at 
sea after their boats were destroyed off Cuddalore. Despite adverse weather, extremely poor visibility and operational limits 
being stretched, the officer volunteered to lead the first-response airborne rescue mission, exemplifying selfless courage and 
resolute leadership. 


3. Demonstrating extraordinary operational planning, the officer meticulously assessed fuel requirements and mission 
parameters, ensuring maximum endurance over the rescue site. At 1515 hours, the ALH Mk-III helicopter launched from 
Chennai International Airport, navigating through persistent weather systems, heavy rain and strong winds, the officer exercised 
flawless Crew Resource Management (CRM) and seamless crew coordination. 


4. Upon reaching the rescue site, the team encountered gale-force winds exceeding 50 knots, significantly reduced 
power margins and dangerously rough seas. Undeterred, the officer executed precise hover and multiple winching operations 
amidst the raging cyclone. His unmatched resilience and flying prowess resulted in the successful rescue of all 10 survivors, 
snatching them from imminent death at sea. 


5. The officer’s extraordinary courage, superior airmanship and unwavering commitment to duty, under life 
threatening conditions, brought immense credit to the Indian Coast Guard. 


6. In recognition of his outstanding valour, unwavering resolve, and superior leadership, 0629-D, Commandant 
Srinivas Gadam has accredited himself well and therefore he is awarded the Tatrakshak Medal (Gallantry). 


7. The Tatrakshak Medal (Gallantry) award is made under Rule 11(i) of the rules governing grant of Tatrakshak Medal 
and consequently carry with them the special allowance admissible under Rule 13 in respect of Coast Guard personnel who 
have received the Tatrakshak Medal (Gallantry) award, i.e, President’s Secretariat Notification No. 50-Pres/89 dated 7th June, 
1989. 


SM SAMI 
Deputy Secretary 


No. 2-Pres/2026—The President is pleased to award the Tatrakshak Medal for Gallantry to 0943-Q, Commandant 
(JG) Ankit Sharma on the occasion of the Independence Day, 2025. 


CITATION 
1. 0943-Q, Commandant (JG) Ankit Sharma, an accomplished and dedicated officer, joined the Indian Coast Guard 
on 30 December 2010. Through his unwavering commitment, professional excellence, and distinguished service, he has earned 
a reputation as a dependable and courageous leader. Presently, he is entrusted with the vital responsibility of Commanding 


Officer of Indian Coast Guard Ship Aruna Asaf Ali, leading his team in safeguarding the nation’s maritime interests with 
utmost dedication and vigilance. 


2. On 23 Nov 2024, acting on a report from a CG aircraft regarding a suspicious vessel in the Indian Exclusive 
Economic Zone (EEZ), 0943-Q, Commandant (JG) Ankit Sharma promptly sailed from Sri Vijaya Puram within an hour, 
despite one main engine being non-operational and prevailing adverse weather. Demonstrating exemplary leadership and 
resolve, the ship located and shadowed the suspect vessel through the night under challenging sea conditions. 


3. Displaying exceptional courage and sound operational judgment, the officer directed the boarding operation during 
the early hours of 24 Nov 2024, 08 NM off Barren Island. His team apprehended the Myanmar-flagged fishing boat with six 
Myanmarese nationals and seized 6,016.87 kg of Methamphetamine, valued at 36,000 crore. Despite heavy rolling that caused 
significant damage to the ship's Gemini craft, his innovative guidance ensured the safe recovery of the boarding team and 
assets.

No. 3-Pres/2026—The President is pleased to award the Tatrakshak Medal for Gallantry to 1095-M, Commandant 
(JG) Rajkamal Attri on the occasion of the Independence Day, 2025. 


CITATION 
1. 1095-M, Commandant (JG) Rajkamal Attri, an accomplished and dedicated officer, joined the Indian Coast Guard 
on 12 June 2012. Through 13 years of distinguished service, he has exhibited exceptional operational acumen, professional 
competence, and steadfast devotion to duty. His proven leadership and operational excellence have led to his present 


appointment as the Commanding Officer of the Indian Coast Guard Ship Agrim, a role demanding courage, sound judgment, 
and the highest degree of responsibility in safeguarding national maritime interests. 


2. On 17 November 2024, the officer displayed exemplary courage and superior tactical judgment during a critical 
maritime operation within India's Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ). The incident arose when a Pakistan Maritime Security 
Agency (PMSA) ship Nusrat, deliberately rammed an Indian fishing boat and unlawfully detained its crew, posing a serious 
threat to the lives of Indian citizens and escalating tensions in a geopolitically sensitive region. 


3. Fully aware of the grave risks, including the potential for armed confrontation, the officer exercised remarkable 
composure and operational brilliance. He manoeuvred ship with precision to swiftly intercept the hostile vessel, adopting an 
assertive posture without provoking aggression. Demonstrating courage and sound diplomatic judgment, he confronted the 
hostile entity through effective communication and skillful negotiation, ultimately securing the unconditional release of the 
Indian fishermen, all while preventing loss of life, avoiding damage to vessels and neutralising the volatile situation without 
resorting to force. 


4. Operation stands as a testament to the officer’s conspicuous act of gallantry, deep understanding of maritime 
diplomacy and exceptional leadership under high-risk conditions. His actions not only safeguarded innocent Indian lives but 
also upheld national sovereignty and preserved peace in a highly sensitive maritime environment. 


5. In recognition of his outstanding valour, unwavering resolve, and superior leadership, 1095-M, Commandant (JG) 
Rajkamal Attri has accredited himself well and therefore he is awarded the Tatrakshak Medal (Gallantry). 


6. The Tatrakshak Medal (Gallantry) award is made under Rule 11(i) of the rules governing grant of Tatrakshak Medal

have received the Tatrakshak Medal (Gallantry) award, i.e, President’s Secretariat Notification No. 50-Pres/89 dated 7th June, 
1989.

MINISTRY OF EDUCATION 
(DEPARTMENT OF HIGHER EDUCATION) 


New Delhi, the 10th February 2026 


No. 10-10/2024-U.3(A)—Whereas, St. Peter’s Institute of Higher Education and Research (Deemed to be University), 
Chennai submitted an online application on UGC Portal to start an off-campus Centre at Hosur, Tamil Nadu by taking over the 
following four affiliated colleges of The Tamil Nadu Dr. M.G.R. Medical University, Chennai, as per the UGC (Institutions 
deemed to be Universities) Regulations, 2023:— 


it St. Peter’s Medical College, Hospital and Research Institute, Hosur 

ii. St. Peter’s Nursing College and Research Institute, Hosur 

ili. St. Peter’s Pharmacy College and Research Institute, Hosur 

iv. St. Peter’s Allied Health Sciences College and Research Institute, Hosur 


2. And whereas, UGC, vide its letter No. 8-19(Delhi)/2025 dated 06.08.2025, informed that the application was 
examined by the UGC through its Standing Committee, after presentation of the Institution and based on the documents 
submitted, recommended for issuance of Letter of Intent (Lol) to St. Peter’s Institute of Higher Education and Research 
(Deemed to be University), Chennai with certain conditions. The recommendation of the Committee was approved by the 
Chairman, UGC. 


3. And further whereas, the Ministry, on the advice of UGC, issued Letter of Intent (Lol) dated 04.12.2025 to 
St. Peter’s Institute of Higher Education and Research (Deemed to be University), Chennai for fulfilment of certain conditions 
within a period of 3 years before starting an off-campus at Hosur, Tamil Nadu. 


4. And whereas, the Registrar, St. Peter’s Institute of Higher Education and Research (Deemed to be University), 
Chennai, vide letter dated 08.12.2025, submitted compliance report in respect of fulfilment of the conditions of the Lol. The 
same was forwarded to UGC for verification and further advice. In response, UGC, vide letter dated 03.02.2026, informed that 
the compliance report was accepted by the Standing Committee and recommended for final approval in the matter. 


5. Now, therefore, in exercise of the powers conferred under Section 3 of the UGC Act, 1956, the Ministry of 
Education, on the advice of UGC, hereby accords approval to St. Peter’s Institute of Higher Education and Research (Deemed 
to be University), Chennai to start an off-campus Centre at Hosur, Tamil Nadu by taking over the four colleges as mentioned 
in para | above. This notification is subject to the final outcome of LPA No.16 of 2026 filed by the Tamil Nadu Dr. M.G.R. 
Medical University Vs. St. Peter’s Institute of Higher Education and Research & Ors. in the Hon’ble High Court of Delhi. 


6. All other conditions mentioned in the earlier Notification(s) of this Ministry as well as the Rules / Regulations of 
UGC and other Statutory Councils, issued from time to time, shall continue to be adhered by St. Peter’s Institute of Higher 
Education and Research (Deemed to be University), Chennai.

S.R.O. 6.— In exercise of the powers conferred by the proviso to article 309 of the Constitution and in 
supersession of the Canteen Stores Department Group ‘C’ (non-industrial and industrial) posts Recruitment Rules, 
99I, in so for as they relate to the post of Stenographer Selection Grade (Stenographer Grade-II) and the Canteen 
Stores Department Stenographer Grade-I posts Recruitment Rules, |999, except as respects things done or omitted to 
be done before such supersession, the President hereby makes the following rules regulating the method of 
recruitment to the post of Stenographer Grade-I in the Canteen Stores Department, Ministry of Defence, namely:- 


I. Short title and commencement .- (l) These rules may be called the Canteen Stores Department, 
Stenographer Grade — I (Group ‘B’ non-gazetted Post) Recruitment Rules, 2026. 


(2) They shall come into force on the date of their publication in the Official Gazette. 


2. Numbers of post, classification and level in pay matrix .- The number of the said post, its classification 
and level in the pay matrix attached thereto shall be as specified in columns (2) to (4) of the Schedule annexed to these 
rules. 


3. Method of recruitment, age-limit, qualifications, etc .-The method of recruitment, age-limit, qualifications 
and the other matters relating to the said post shall be as specified in columns (5) to ((3) of the said Schedule. 


4. Disqualification .- No person,- 
(a) who has entered into or contracted a marriage with any person having a spouse living; or 
(b) who, having a spouse living, has entered into or contracted a marriage with any person, 
shall be eligible for appointment to the said post: 


Provided that the Central Government may, if satisfied that such marriage is permissible under the personal 
law applicable to such person and other party to the marriage and that there are other grounds for so doing, exempt 
any person from the operation of this rule. 


5. Power to relax: - Where the Central Government is of the opinion that it is necessary or expedient so to do, 
it may, by order and for reasons to be recorded in writing, relax any of the provisions of these rules with respect to any 
class or category of persons. 


6. Saving: - Nothing in these rules shall affect reservation, relaxation of age-limit and other concessions 
required to be provided for the Scheduled Castes, the Scheduled Tribes, the Other Backward Classes, the Ex- 
servicemen and other special categories of persons in accordance with the orders issued by the Central Government 
from time to time in this regard.

G.S.R. 50.—In exercise of the powers conferred by the proviso to Article 309 of the Constitution, the 
President hereby makes the following rules regulating the method of recruitment to the Group ‘C’, Non- Gazetted 
post of Upper Division Clerk (Level-4) in the Department of Space, namely:- 


l. Short title and commencement - (l) These rules are called the Department of Space, Upper Division Clerk 
Recruitment Rules, 2025. 


(2) They shall come into force on the date of their publication in the Official Gazette. 


2. Application — These rules shall apply to the posts as specified in column () of the Schedule annexed to these 
rules. 


3. Number of posts, classification and Levels in the Pay Matrix — The number of the said posts, classification and 
Levels in the Pay Matrix attached thereto shall be as specified in columns (2) to (4) of the Schedule annexed to 
these rules. 


4. Method of recruitment, age limit, qualification, etc.- | The method of recruitment, age limit, qualification and 
other matters relating to the said post shall be as specified in columns (5) to (3) of the said Schedule. 


5. Disqualification — No person, - 
(a) who has entered into or contracted a marriage with a person having spouse living; 
OR 
(b) who, having a spouse living, has entered into or contracted a marriage with any person, 
shall be eligible for appointment to any of the said posts: 


Provided that the Central Government may, if satisfied that such marriage is permissible under the personal law 
applicable to such person and the other party to the marriage and that there are other grounds for so doing, 
exempt any person from the operation of this rule. 


6. Power to relax - Where the Central Government is of the opinion that it is necessary or expedient to do so, it may, 
by order and for reasons to be recorded in writing, relax any of the provisions of these rules with respect to any 
class or category of persons.

G.S.R. 54.—In exercise of the powers conferred by the proviso to Article 309 of the Constitution, the 
President hereby makes the following rules regulating the method of recruitment to Group ‘B’, Non-Gazetted post of 
Personal Assistant (Level 7) in the Department of Space, namely:- 


l. Short title and commencement — (l) These rules are called the Department of Space, Personal Assistant 
Recruitment Rules, 2025. 


(2) They shall come into force on the date of their publication in the Official Gazette. 


2. Application — These rules shall apply to the posts as specified in column (l) of the Schedule annexed to these 
tules. 


3. Number of posts, classification and Levels in the Pay Matrix — The number of the said posts, classification and 
Levels in the Pay Matrix attached thereto shall be as specified in columns (2) to (4) of the Schedule annexed to 


these rules. 


4. Method of recruitment, age limit, qualification, etc. -The method of recruitment, age limit, qualification and 
other matters relating to the said post shall be as specified in columns (5) to (I3) of the said Schedule. 


5. Disqualification — No person, - 
(a) who has entered into or contracted a marriage with a person having spouse living; 
OR 
(b) who, having a spouse living, has entered into or contracted a marriage with any person, 
shall be eligible for appointment to any of the said posts: 
Provided that the Central Government may, if satisfied that such marriage is permissible under the personal law 
applicable to such person and the other party to the marriage and that there are other grounds for so doing, 
exempt any person from the operation of this rule. 

6. Power to relax - Where the Central Government is of the opinion that it is necessary or expedient to do so, it may, 
by order and for reasons to be recorded in writing, relax any of the provisions of these rules with respect to any 
class or category of persons. 

7. Saving — Nothing in these rules shall affect reservations, relaxation of age limit and other concessions required to 
be provided for the Scheduled Castes, the Scheduled Tribes, the Other Backward Classes, Ex-servicemen and 


other special categories of persons in accordance with the orders issued by the Central Government from time to 
time in this regard.

G.S.R. 55.—In exercise of the powers conferred by the proviso to Article 309 of the Constitution, the 
President hereby makes the following rules regulating the method of recruitment to Group ‘B’, Gazetted post of 
Private Secretary (Level-8) in the Department of Space, namely:- 


l. Short title and commencement - (l) These rules are called the Department of Space, Private Secretary 
Recruitment Rules, 2025. 


(2) They shall come into force on the date of their publication in the Official Gazette. 


2. Application — These rules shall apply to the posts as specified in column (l) of the Schedule annexed to these 
rules. 


3. Number of posts, classification and Levels in the Pay Matrix — The number of the said posts, classification and 
Levels in the Pay Matrix attached thereto shall be as specified in columns (2) to (4) of the Schedule annexed to 
these rules. 


4. Method of recruitment, age limit, qualification, etc.- | The method of recruitment, age limit, qualification and 
other matters relating to the said post shall be as specified in columns (5) to (I3) of the said Schedule. 


5. Disqualification — No person, - 
(a) who has entered into or contracted a marriage with a person having spouse living; 
OR 


(b) who, having a spouse living, has entered into or contracted a marriage with any person,

Provided that the Central Government may, if satisfied that such marriage is permissible under the personal law 
applicable to such person and the other party to the marriage and that there are other grounds for so doing, 
exempt any person from the operation of this rule. 


6. Power to relax - Where the Central Government is of the opinion that it is necessary or expedient to do so, it may, 
by order and for reasons to be recorded in writing, relax any of the provisions of these rules with respect to any 
class or category of persons. 


7. Saving — Nothing in these rules shall affect reservations, relaxation of age limit and other concessions required to 
be provided for the Scheduled Castes, the Scheduled Tribes, the Other Backward Classes, Ex-servicemen and 
other special categories of persons in accordance with the orders issued by the Central Government from time to 
time in this regard.

(a) who has entered into or contracted a marriage with a person having spouse living; 
OR 
(b) who, having a spouse living, has entered into or contracted a marriage with any person, 
shall be eligible for appointment to any of the said posts: 


Provided that the Central Government may, if satisfied that such marriage is permissible under the personal law 
applicable to such person and the other party to the marriage and that there are other grounds for so doing, 
exempt any person from the operation of this rule.

by order and for reasons to be recorded in writing, relax any of the provisions of these rules with respect to any

be provided for the Scheduled Castes, the Scheduled Tribes, the Other Backward Classes, Ex-servicemen and 
other special categories of persons in accordance with the orders issued by the Central Government from time to 
time in this regard.

G.S.R. 62.—In exercise of the powers conferred by the proviso to Article 309 of the Constitution, the 
President hereby makes the following rules regulating the method of recruitment to the Group ‘C’, Non-Gazetted post 
of Multi-Tasking Staff (Level-) in the Department of Space, namely:

l. Short title and commencement - (l) These rules are called the Department of Space, Multi-Tasking Staff 
Recruitment Rules, 2025. 


(2) They shall come into force on the date of their publication in the Official Gazette. 


2. Application — These rules shall apply to the posts as specified in column () of the Schedule annexed to these 
rules. 


3. Number of posts, classification and Levels in the Pay Matrix — The number of the said posts, classification and 
Levels in the Pay Matrix attached thereto shall be as specified in columns (2) to (4) of the Schedule annexed to 
these rules. 


4. Method of recruitment, age limit, qualification, etc.- | The method of recruitment, age limit, qualification and 
other matters relating to the said post shall be as specified in columns (5) to (3) of the said Schedule. 


5. Disqualification — No person, - 
(a) who has entered into or contracted a marriage with a person having spouse living; 
OR 
(b) who, having a spouse living, has entered into or contracted a marriage with any person, 
shall be eligible for appointment to any of the said posts: 


Provided that the Central Government may, if satisfied that such marriage is permissible under the personal law 
applicable to such person and the other party to the marriage and that there are other grounds for so doing, 
exempt any person from the operation of this rule. 


6. Power to relax - Where the Central Government is of the opinion that it is necessary or expedient to do so, it may, 
by order and for reasons to be recorded in writing, relax any of the provisions of these rules with respect to any 
class or category of persons. 


7. Saving — Nothing in these rules shall affect reservations, relaxation of age limit and other concessions required to 
be provided for the Scheduled Castes, the Scheduled Tribes, the Other Backward Classes, Ex-servicemen and 
other special categories of persons in accordance with the orders issued by the Central Government from time to 
time in this regard.

2. इसके द्वारा यह सूचित किया जाता है कि कम्पनी अधिनियम, 2043 की धारा 248 (2) के तहत कम्पनी रजिस्ट्रार को उपर्युक्त 
कम्पनियों के नाम कम्पनी रजिस्टर से इस आधार पर नाम हटाने का आवेदन प्राप्त हुआ है कि कम्पनी के निगमन के एक वर्ष के भीतर कारोबार 
आरंभ करने में विफल रहे हैं या इस आधार पर कि कम्पनी पूर्ववर्ती 2 वित्तीय वर्षों से कारोबार नहीं कर पाई है और इस अवधि के भीतर कम्पनी 
अधिनियम, 2043 की धारा 455 के तहत निष्क्रिय कम्पनी की स्थिति प्राप्त करने का आदेश का आवेदन नहीं किया है या कम्पनी ने निष्क्रिय 
कम्पनी की स्थिति प्राप्त कर ली है, पर वे कम्पनी के रुप में पंजीकरण नहीं रखना चाहते और अतः कम्पनी रजिस्ट्रार से अपना/अपने नाम हटाने

आरंभ करने में विफल रहे हैं या इस आधार पर कि कम्पनी पूर्ववर्ती 2 वित्तीय वर्षों से कारोबार नहीं कर पाई है और इस अवधि के भीतर कम्पनी 
अधिनियम, 2043 की धारा 455 के तहत निष्क्रिय कम्पनी की स्थिति प्राप्त करने का आदेश का आवेदन नहीं किया है या कम्पनी ने निष्क्रिय 
कम्पनी की स्थिति प्राप्त कर ली है, पर वे कम्पनी के रुप में पंजीकरण नहीं रखना चाहते और अतः कम्पनी रजिस्ट्रार से अपना/अपने नाम हटाने

2. इसके द्वारा यह सूचित किया जाता है कि कम्पनी अधिनियम, 2043 की धारा 248 (2) के तहत कम्पनी रजिस्ट्रार को उपर्युक्त 
कम्पनियों के नाम कम्पनी रजिस्टर से इस आधार पर नाम हटाने का आवेदन प्राप्त हुआ है कि कम्पनी के निगमन के एक वर्ष के भीतर कारोबार 
आरंभ करने में विफल रहे हैं या इस आधार पर कि कम्पनी पूर्ववर्ती 2 वित्तीय वर्षों से कारोबार नहीं कर पाई है और इस अवधि के भीतर कम्पनी 
अधिनियम, 2043 की धारा 455 के तहत निष्क्रिय कम्पनी की स्थिति प्राप्त करने का आदेश का आवेदन नहीं किया है या कम्पनी ने निष्क्रिय 
कम्पनी की स्थिति प्राप्त कर ली है, पर वे कम्पनी के रुप में पंजीकरण नहीं रखना चाहते और अतः कम्पनी रजिस्ट्रार से अपना/अपने नाम हटाने 
का अनुरोध किया है। 

3. तदनुसार, कम्पनी रजिस्ट्रार उपर्युक्त कम्पनियों के नामों को कम्पनियों के रजिस्टर से हटाने का प्रस्ताव करता है। 

4. यदि किसी व्यक्ति/संस्था को कम्पनी को कम्पनी रजिस्ट्रार से कम्पनियों का नाम हटाने के प्रस्ताव से आपत्ति है तो वह व्यक्ति/संस्था 
इस सूचना के प्रकाशन की तारीख से 30 (तीस) दिनों के भीतर उपर्युक्त कार्यालय के पते पर अपनी आपत्ति भेज सकते हैं |

reads : 


“the object and purport of principle of res judicata as contained in Section l of Code Of Civil 
Procedure is to uphold the rule of conclusiveness of judgement. As to the points decided earlier of fact, 
or of law, or of fact and law, in every subsequent suit between the same parties. Once the matter which 
was the subject matter of list stood determined by a competent court, no party thereafter can be 
permitted to re-open it in a subsequent litigation. Such a rule was brought into the statute book with a 
view to bring the litigation to an end so that the otherside may not be put to harassment. 


The Principle of res judicata that a judgement of a court of concurrent jurisdiction directly upon a point 
would create a bar as regards a plea, between the same parties in some other matter in another court, 
where the said plea seeks to raise afresh the very point that was determined in the earlier judgement.” 


In Gulab Chand Chotalal Parikh vs. State of Gujarat (AIR 965 SC 453), the constitution bench of the Hon’ble 
Apex Court held that the principles of res judicata is also applicable to subsequent suits where the same issues 
between the same parties had been decided in an earlier proceeding under Article 226 of the Constitution.

2I. It is a settled principle of law that a decision by the Hon’ble High Court in Writ Petitions under Article 226 
are subjected to res judicata and binding the parties in later litigation reinforcing Section |l of the Code of Civil 
Procedure. In essense, a binding decision of Hon’ble High Court brings closure to that specific dispute fostering 
judicial efficiency and preventing endless litigation. 


22. The Hon’ble Apex Court in Pooja Ferro Alloys Pvt. Ltd vs. State of Goa c/w others (2025 INSC 27) 
concurrently quoted the following principle from Satyadhyan Ghosal vs. Deorajin Debi (960 3 SCR 590) 


“The principle of res judicata is based on the need of giving a finality to judicial decisions. What it says 
is that once a res is judicata, it shall not be adjudged again. Primarily it applies as between past 
litigation and future litigation. When a matter — whether on a question of fact or a question of law — 
has been decided between two parties in one suit or proceeding and the decision is final, either because 
no appeal was taken to a higher court or because the appeal was dismissed, or no appeal lies, neither 
party will be allowed in a future suit or proceeding between the same parties to canvass the matter 
again. This principle of res judicata is embodied in relation to suits in Section I of the Code of Civil 
Procedure; but even where Section does not apply, the principle of res judicata has been applied by 
courts for the purpose of achieving finality in litigation. The result of this is that the original court as 
well as any higher court must in any future litigation proceed on the basis that the previous decision was 
correct. 


The principle of res judicata applies also as between two stages in the same litigation to this extent that a 
court, whether the trial court or a higher court having at an earlier stage decided a matter in one way 
will not allow the parties to re-agitate the matter again at a subsequent stage of the same proceedings. 


99 
ee 


In Pooja Ferro case supra, the Hon’ble Apex Court with reference to the verdict of the Hon’ble High Court of Kerala 
in T P Moideen Koya vs. State of Kerala (2004 8 SCC 06) held that the principle of res judicata applies even to 
the petitions arising for decision in the writ jurisdiction under Article 226 of the constitution. 


23. The I Party relied upon the ruling of the Hon’ble High Court of Calcutta in M/s. Supreme and Co. vs. Netai 
Bhaduri and another in WP No. 3544/2002 with CAN 2334/20I4 and also Ms. Anita vs. The Presiding Officer, 
Labour Court, Ambala and another (CWP No. 2825/206) dated 3.05.2024. The first ruling M/s. Supreme cited 
supra is on the subject of an Award passed by the Industrial Tribunal, West Bengal. The said ruling directly is not of 
any help to the Appellant herein as, the question of res judicata under consideration herein is in view of the findings 
of the higher courts. In the second citation Ms. Anita Case supra ofcourse, the finding rendered by the Central 
Administrative Tribunal in a service matter of an Employee is rendered as nullity holding that the issue is beyond the 
jurisdictional competence of the CAT, whereas in the given case the fairness of the Domestic Enquiry proceedings 
and the eventual punishment imposed by the Disciplinary Authority were directly put under challenge before the 
Hon’ble High Court of Karnataka invoking the provisions of Article 226 of the Constitution of India. Though 
initially succeeded in the Writ Petition, the case of the I Party was turned down by the successive verdicts in the Writ 
Appeal and the Special Leave Petition. Since the verdict passed by the Hon’ble High Court invoking Article 226 and 
227 has a binding effect on the Principle of Res judicata, those verdicts are binding on the parties to the litigations, 
conclusively putting an end to the dispute raised and prohibiting a further re-agitation of the same issue. Therefore, I 
am of the considered view that the present industrial dispute raised by the I Party is barred by the Principle of res 
judicata. With this view, Preliminary Issue No. 2 is answered against the I Party.

The I Party then raised an Industrial Dispute through Union before the Conciliation Officer under the ID Act. 
Based on the report of failure submitted by the Conciliation Officer, the Central Government referred the matter to

5. The II Party in its written statement per contra contended that the towards the Leave Fair Concession applied

personal use alone, the I Party was asked to produce the bill / receipts of his lodging at the places where he claimed to

6. From the above rival pleadings, the points arising for determination are: 


a) Issue no. 0l: Whether the I Party is able to demonstrate the finding of the Enquiry Officer as baseless or

b) Issue no. 2: If not, whether the punishment of reduction in scale of pay by two stages with cumulative effect

7 Issue no. l: Indisputably, the I Party while working as clerk in the II Party Bank at its Malleshwaram branch 
applied for LFC claiming Rs. 25,000/- and availed a sum of Rs. !9,000/- as advance. Payment of advance was subject

on rental basis during the period in question. To buttress its case, II party has relied upon Ex M-6 (Enquiry

8. On a perusal of the enquiry report submitted by the Enquiry Officer, it is clear that he has examined each and

9. While analysing the photograph of the tourage furnished by the I Party, the Enquiry Officer very pertinently 
noted that though all the members of the family including wife, children and mother of the I Party are shown as the 
persons accompanying in the tourage, the photographs do not reveal the co-passengers. As rightly observed by the 
Enquiry Officer, this is the crucial aspect when judged in the shady and suspicious scenario relating to the 
manipulations regarding the vehicles allegedly used for undertaking the journey. The evidence of the witness 
examined from the side of the management to prove the documents is closely analysed and scrutinized by the Enquiry 
Officer in his enquiry report. The Domestic Enquiry records would indicate that the I Party himself raised an 
argument before the Enquiry Officer that he was not in the know-how that M/s Durga Travels had no proper permit as

authorized travel agent. Having taken the task of producing Ex M4 and M5 series to his employer under the hand and 
seal of Sri Durga Travels to assert that he has undertaken tourage through the said travel, it is quite anomalous for him 
to urge that the said travel agency is not an authorized travel agent. As a responsible employee, he should be aware of 
the fact that travel documents from travel agencies through whom the tour program was undertaken is a very essential 
and genuine document to be produced before the authority to claim Leave Fare Concession (LFC). The material 
alteration in Ex M 5/I referred to above being so glaring, apparent and patent, not at all authenticated or duly

0. The I Party has emphatically blamed the II Party for the non-examination of Sh. L T Vijayaendra, the then 
Manager, Bank of Maharashtra, who conducted initial investigation in the matter and submitted Ex M 7/I report dated 
5.09.998 to the Branch Manager, Bank of Maharashtra. Of course, the said Manager is not seen examined during 
the domestic enquiry. What he has brought out in his report Ex M 7/I is that :- 


(.) Vehicle no. KA 02 — N 8585 is a Maruti Zen car registered for private use only; 
(2) The owner had denied having allowed the said car for public conducted tours and; 
(3) M/s Durga Travel - travel agency is not engaging private vehicles to conduct public tours. 


ll. Actually, the II Party has brought in evidence Ex M [7, the copy of a letter sent by the Branch Manager 
dated 4.09.998 to aforementioned Sh. G V Srinivasa Murthi, Vijayanagar Bangalore, seeking confirmation with 
particulars whether his vehicle bearing no. KA 02 — N 8585 was let out for travelling purpose from 07.04.998 to 
28.04.998 for LTC purpose to M/s Durga Travels, Bangalore. Ex M-8 is the reply given by Sh. G V Srinivasa 
Murthi that the aforesaid vehicle (Maruti car) is for his private cum personal use and he has not let it to any travel 
agency for conducting any public tours at any time. Since the owner himself has declared the fact that the vehicle 
aforementioned is a private car and the same has not been let to any travel agency for conducting any public tour at 
any time, non-examination of Sh. L T Vijayaendra, the Manager in the domestic enquiry is not that crucial or 
significant, nor his examination caused any detriment to the action initiated by the management against the workman. 
The enquiry records would indicate that sufficient opportunity was given to the I Party to produce the RTO permit in 
respect of the vehicle said to have been used for undertaking the tour / journey and he did not produce the same at any 
point of time. ७४], the Manager, testified that he himself has visited the office of M/s Durga Travels for verification 
of the bills submitted by the I Party and he was informed by the employee of M/s Durga Travels that the persons 
employed during April-May !998 have been discontinued and the records of that period are not available for 
reference or for confirmation. On a perusal of the enquiry records, I am convinced that all valid and essential piece of 
evidence has been let in by the II Party management in the domestic enquiry proceedings which strongly establish that 
the I Party has brought in fake and forged documents to claim LFC benefits and obtained a sum of Rs. 9,000/- by 3 
occasions from the management. None of the counter arguments set forth by the I Party in this regard is capable of 
defeating the case of the II Party. 


2. Another emphatic argument raised on behalf of the I Party is that the charge sheet has been issued to him by 
an incompetent person whereas it ought to have been issued by the Chief Manager and therefore the charge sheet is 
void and the enquiry conducted on such void charge sheet is liable to be set aside and no sanctity could be attached to 
such an enquiry. It is equally urged that the enquiry conducted being so, the punishment imposed on the I Party 
workman on such a charge sheet is liable to be set aside. Of course, Ex M I/! charge sheet dated 23.09.2003 is seen 
issued by the disciplinary authority and Dy. General Manager, Bangalore region. The contention raised by the I Party 
alleging incompetency on the authority who issued the charge sheet is vehemently opposed by the learned counsel for 
the वा Party voicing that it is not all the more required that the authority competent to impose penalty itself must 
initiate disciplinary proceedings. In P V Srinivasa Sastry and others vs. Comptroller & Auditor General and 
others (AIR 993 SC 32), the Hon'ble Apex Court held that “In absence of a Rule, any superior authority who can 
be held to be the controlling authority, can initiate such proceeding.” On a later occasion in Inspector General of 
Police and another vs. Thavasiappan (AIR 996 SC 38) also, the Hon'ble Apex Court held that in the absence of 
any specific rule, the initiation of proceedings by an authority higher in rank to the delinquent is not vitiated and it is 
not necessary always that the departmental proceeding is to be initiated only by the appointing authority. 


3. The Hon'ble Apex Court in Steel Authority of India and another vs. Dr Diwakar and others (AIR 998 
SC 220) concurred and quoted the following from Director General, ESI & Anr vs T. Abdul Razak (996 SCC 
(4) 708) which reads :- 


“it is not necessary that the authority competent to impose the penalty must initiate the disciplinary 
proceedings and that the proceedings can be initiated by any superior authority who can be held to be the 
controlling authority who may be an officer subordinate to the appointing authority.” 


4. Following the above afore cited rulings of the Hon'ble Apex Court , the Hon’ble High Court of Madras in 
Superintending Engineer, Madurai vs. Presiding Officer, Labour Court (WP 0097 of 995 dated 0.03.2002) 
held that :- 


834 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : FEBRUARY 2], 2026/PHALGUNA 2, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


“It is obvious that such a proceedings could have been initiated by the Controlling Authority even though 
he is not the appointing authority.” 


5. In view of this legal principle enunciated in the rulings cited supra , the contention raised and the argument 
advanced by the I Party challenging and questioning the competency of the Dy. General Manager who issued the 
charge sheet is absolutely untenable and unsustainable. Accordingly, no evil consequence should follow in respect of 
the action initiated by the Disciplinary Authority against the I Party. 


6. Another fold of argument raised by the I Party is that the disciplinary action initiated by the II party stood 
unreasonably delayed and hence he could not get the requisite documents from the aforementioned travel agency to 
defend his case. Of course, the LFC application was submitted by him in the year 4998 for the block period 998 to 
2002 to avail the facility from 07.04.998 till 26.04.998. Eventual to the production of Ex M4 and ३5/।, the so 
called final receipt cum certificates of journey which raised a lot of suspicion and anomalous features, the 
management went on making its own investigations and recurrently requested the I Party to produce RTO permit 
copy in respect of the vehicle which he allegedly used for his tour journey. Till 2002 the anomalous factors were not 
got clarified by the I party. Instead, as per Ex M-8 dated 2.02.2002 in response to the II Party’s letter dated 
29.0.2002 calling for explanation from him regarding the number of the bus in which he had travelled under LFC , 
he has stated to the II Party that the second bill (Ex ॥३/) is submitted by him as the vehicle number in the earlier bill 
contained a typographical error. The resubmitted bill is nothing other than Ex ३5/| which obviously is a manipulated, 
fabricated and materially altered document as apparent on the face of it. Ex M5/2 cash receipt dated 07.04.998 by 
Sri Durga Travels acknowledging Rs. 25000/- bears receipt no. !488 which is quoted in Ex M5/I, the forged 
document. Ex M5/2 receipt also becomes a shady document since a different receipt number viz., |897 is seen written 
in Ex M4 final receipt. 


7. So the reply submitted by him in 2002 also did not reconcile the issue. Though he was specifically asked as 
early as on 4.05.998 to produce |) RTO Permit copy number, 2) Lodge bill as a proof of stay, 3) Stamp receipt for 
Rs. 25000/- and 4) Original receipt number !897 mentioned in the bill (Ex M4), he did not comply with the direction 
at all. Again the II Party has continued correspondences with him in writing. Instead of adhering to the direction, he 
preferred to send letter dated 04.06.998 Ex M-I] demanding an additional advance of Rs. 2000/- to meet an urgent 
need to pay off the Karnataka Electricity Bill amount, assuring that he would submit RTO and LFC bill certificate on 
the next day. Honouring the urgent need expressed by him, the II Party management has sanctioned an additional 
advance of Rs. 2000/-, thereby making the total advance so far disbursed as Rs. !7000/-. All the continued 
communications issued by the II Party to him requiring production of the crucial documents did meet with no positive 
response from him. However, an additional advance of Rs. 2000/- was sanctioned by the II Party during April 200], 
making the total LFC advance disbursed to the I Party as Rs. [9000/-. As per the letter dated 8.07.200], the Assistant 
General Manager, Bangalore region has addressed the Branch Manager of the I Party bank to reject the LFC bill for 
the discrepancies between Ex M4 and M5 bills submitted by the I Party rendering the identity of the vehicle 
absolutely vague and suspicious and to recover the entire advance disbursed under LFC scheme to the I Party. The 
said matter was informed by the Branch Manager to the I Party as per Ex M2! letter dated 25.07.200! requiring him 
to pay back the advance with interest immediately. In response to the above intimation, the I Party sent Ex M22 letter 
dated 05.08.200l requesting to give Xerox copies of the LFC bills submitted by him in April 998. Since the 
captioned bills were sent to the regional office by way of endorsement in Ex M22, the Branch Manager made a 
request to the regional office to make the copies available to the delinquent staff. Conversely on getting Xerox copies 
of the LFC bills, the I Party under Ex M-23 letter dated 09.0.200l informed the Branch Manager that the bill 
submitted by him are genuine and the same should be reimbursed immediately. This fact was in turn intimated to the 
Assistant General Manager by the Branch Manager as per Ex M24 letter dated 2.0.200. Then on 24.0.2002 as per 
Ex M 25/I notice, explanation was called for from the I Party by the Assistant General Manager specifically narrating 
the discrepancies in the bills on its preliminary appraisal that he has committed misconducts relating to availing of 
LFC facility. The II Party management has waited for a considerable time for his explanation. As there was no reply 
from him, ultimately the II Party has initiated the disciplinary proceedings against the I Party by appointing the 
Enquiry Officer and the Presenting Officer. 


8. Reckoning the umpteen number of communications / intimations sent by the II party to the I party 
successively in sequence calling upon him to produce necessary documents to sanction the LFC bill and the assurance 
made by him to adhere to the direction and the negation / refusal of the I Party thenceforth, I do not find any wilfull or 
deliberate delay on the part of the II Party management to initiate the proceedings. 


9. The contention of the I Party that due to the delay he could not collect necessary evidence to support his 
defence from the travel agency is absolutely untenable and unsustainable for the very reason that ample opportunities 
were accorded to him to produce relevant documents from the concerned and he simply negated or rather ignored it. 
Instead all along he has been commanding the management to sanction his LFC bills for the rest of the amount 
claimed. Had he been so vigilant to collect valid evidence from the travel agency and the Regional Transport 
Authorities, he could have certainly done it at a very early point of time when the II Party has expressed unfaith and 
severe suspicion in respect of the documents Ex M4 and ३5/ and M5/2 produced by him. Apart, no attempt has 
been made by him to put in an application before the Enquiry Officer to summon the authority concerned of Sri Durga
